subsubtopic: DEGREE OF CANADIAN COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on Monday the leaders of two of NATO's most important member nations spoke of the need for tough action to counter the growing Soviet threat to world peace. The British Prime
Minister proclaimed that aggression must never be allowed to pay and that it is time for freedom to take the offensive. The American President warned that we cannot count on the instinct for survival to protect us against war. However, our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) believes that the survival of our species depends on the courage and wisdom of nations and their leaders. Does he truly believe that courage and wisdom will stop the Soviet threat any more than appeasement stopped Hitler?
The Prime Minister signed a friendship protocol agreement with the U.S.S.R. in 1971 and proclaimed that Canadians find themselves living within a constitutional framework with a formal structure similar to that in the Soviet Union. He has also stated that he would choose Cuban or Chinese socialism as the national model for Canadian society, and he has led communist delegations to Moscow and Peking.
Is this why Canada ranks thirteenth out of the 14 NATO nations in defence spending? Is this why the Prime Minister vacillated for months before announcing a boycott of the Olympics after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, and why he has been silent in the House on the Soviet destruction of a Korean airliner?
1 call upon the Prime Minister to rise in his place and declare Canada's commitment to NATO's efforts to match Soviet might with western might, or to state whether he is in fact still a communist sympathizer.

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS BY MINISTER S OFFICE OVER PUBLICATION OFCARTOON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to draw to the attention of the House what I consider to be a very serious example of interference with freedom of the press by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola). Recently an article and cartoon appeared in a newsletter published by the Native Women's Association of Canada which depicted a massacre of Indian peasants by government troops in Guatemala. The cartoon was in fact drawn by an Indian child who had survived this massacre.
The office of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs blatantly interfered with freedom of the press by contacting the office of the Native Women's Association of Canada and suggesting to this organization that perhaps the cartoon did not reflect the policy of the Government of Canada. The Minister in question, Madam Speaker, indicated

September 28, 1983
that she felt that the cartoon was not in particularly good taste and was not relevant to that particular magazine.
I do not think that I have to remind Members of the House of Commons that in a free society, a society with freedom of the press, it is political thuggery for a Minister of the Crown to contact an organization about a newsletter which is partly government financed and suggest to that organization that she does not approve of their editorial policy, whether it be in cartoons or elsewhere. This is particularly serious in light of this Minister's responsibility for implementing the recommendations of the Kent Commission and bringing forward legislation that could touch upon freedom of the press. I am sure all members of the House would join with me in condemning this very heavy handed action-

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF SECOND CAREER ASSISTANCE NETWORK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 would like to call to the attention of the House the fact that every year over 4,000 servicemen leave the Canadian Armed Forces because of compulsory retirement provisions or medical problems. The vast majority of these men and women are between 40 and 50 years of age, with some having only a primary school education. These service people may find themselves at the termination of their service with few marketable skills in Civilian life. The individuals who are fortunate enough to learn a skill will find that only one-third of the 110 trades available within the Armed Forces are recognized by provincial trade associations.
Serious consideration should be given by the Government of Canada to a meaningful increase in the funding of the second career assistance network currently administered by the Department of National Defence, along with a redirection of that program to assist those who face the greatest difficulty instead of those individuals who are easiest to place in civilian life.
At the same time the Government of Canada should consider, as a priority, the establishment of a Canadian Armed Forces technical school that would meet the educational requirements of the Provinces in skilled training and assist Canadian industry in averting shortages of skilled labour in the 1980s.

subsubtopic: COST OF ESTABLISHING HELICOPTER MANUFACTURING IN PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
The late Right Hon. John Diefen-baker once made the following statement, "I have but one love, Canada; one purpose, its greatness; one aim, unity from the Atlantic to the Pacific." These are indeed inspiring words- words which should be brought to mind regularly.
As a Member of Parliament, 1 feel it incumbent upon myself to bring up issues which affect the lives of Canadians and the unity of the country. Madam Speaker, the issue is one of fairness. In order for citizens to regain feelings of unity and harmony within Confederation, people in every Province must feel that they are receiving their share of the benefits from the federal Government.
The Hon. Member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) once spoke of the Liberal team in Quebec as one that will promote the interests of all Quebecers and indeed, all Canadians. If the Liberal Party is one that serves all Canadians, then why does the Government intend to set up helicopter manfacturing facilities in Quebec at a cost to the taxpayers of Canada of $500 million? This decision was taken despite the fact that alternate, cheaper facilities are available.
Fleet Industries in Fort Erie, a firm with a reputation as an aeronautical pioneer, can provide the same service with startup costs of only $35 million. Not only that, but many more jobs would be going to Canadians. Bell is an American firm, whose R and D will take place primarily in the United States. The proposal by Fleet Industries of Fort Erie will bring more jobs to Canadians and will cost much less.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL FUNDING OF SECOND LANGUAGE EDUCATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, between 1978 and the present the federal Government has reduced its commitment to the Provinces for funding second language education, with the result that the Provinces are putting up more and more of the costs. What this means is that the number of students who can be educated in their second language, and the number of Canadians who can be employed in assisting Canadian children to become bilingual, declines dramatically.
Yesterday, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced that "Co-operative federalism is dead-and will remain dead in the sense that the federal Government is expected to hand money over to the Provinces for them to spend in any which
September 28, 1983

way." In this case, the cuts in federal funding in real terms would imply that, if co-operative federalism is dead, it is the Trudeau Government that has killed it.
If the Government believes that one of the hallmarks of the particular nature of federalism in Canada is the commitment of all citizens to a bilingual country, then it will have to explain how it expects Canadian citizens to support and entrench official bilingualism when, at the same time, the federal Government cuts funds for bilingual education and makes it more and more difficult for Canadian children to become competent in their second official language. We in the New Democratic Party urge the Government to commit itself to long-term funding for bilingual education.

If the federal Government is serious about bilingualism in Canada, it must take the necessary action and grant financial assistance to schools, across Canada, in order to achieve this goal.

subsubtopic: HIRING OF AMERICAN MARKETING ANALYSTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Funk and Wagnall's dictionary defines irony as the reverse of what is expected. I have just learned of a situation which Canadian taxpayers will agree is not only dripping with irony-it is bizarre.
CBC's AM station in Edmonton, CBX, has experienced a serious decline in audience ratings recently. Listeners prefer Ron Collister's talk show on CJCA, or Standard Broadcast News coverage on CFRN. At any rate, the high-powered commercial competition in Edmonton was apparently too much for mother corporation.
The CBC's answer was to hire media marketing consultants to lure listeners to CBX, to gear up for ratings week, which is happening right now in Edmonton. The slight problem is that the CBC hired two, possibly three, market analysts from Chicago, Illinois. At heaven knows what expense to the Canadian taxpayer, the firm of Reimer and Gerson spent several weeks surveying 18 to 35 year olds in the Edmonton market.
I find this astonishing and shameful. Surely the hundreds of millions of dollars we taxpayers pump into the CBC could produce either corporation expertise or, at least, Canadian media marketing talent to survey Edmonton or any other place in Canada.
The irony of this situation is that the CBC, with its pronounced nationalistic and anti-U.S. bias, should go to the Americans to tell Canadians what we are all about.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-IMPORTATION OF HIGH SULPHUR CONTENT COAL FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of the Environment. It concerns both the problems of acid rain and the need to create more jobs.
Is the Acting Prime Minister aware that the Province of Ontario imports, from the United States, 80 per cent of the coal that it requires, coal which has eight times the sulphur content, sulphur being the active producer of acid rain, as does coal coming from western Canada? If he is aware of this fact will he try to persuade Premier Davis, who is always speaking of the need to buy Canadian, to practise what he preaches, stop getting his coal from the United States and, instead, buy it from western Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-IMPORTATION OF HIGH SULPHUR CONTENT COAL FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps because I have some past familiarity with these questions, I could respond to the Hon. Member. It has been the case that we in Canada have been pressing, both on the Provinces and on Governments outside Canada, namely, the United States' Government, actions which would lead to the appropriate level of emissions to control the problem of acid rain.
The approach we have always taken has been not to try to prescribe the methods of arriving at these objectives, but, rather, to establish the objective which is acceptable and then leave to the responsible jurisdictions whatever means they wish to pursue to arrive at that reasonable objective. Instead of trying to prescribe the means to establish what needs to be done, we leave to the responsible jurisdiction the means of arriving at it.
There is a context, under the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, of committees which leads the federal Government to be in continual discussion with all of the Provinces, including Ontario, concerning how to respond to the needs of bringing down the Canadian emission level which will lead to safe results. The whole question involving utilization of coal and the kind of coal has been an essential matter within those discussions.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXPAND SECTORAL FREE TRADE WITH UNITED STATES
PROPOSAL TO EXPAND SECTORAL FREE TRADE WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for International Trade. It concerns the paper "Canadian Trade Policy for the 1980s" which he introduced about a month ago. When the Minister was commenting on the paper, he said that we need more sector by sector free trade agreements with the United States. About 11 years ago one of his predecessors, Mitchell Sharp, said in a similar paper that the free trade option "was judged to be inconsistent with Canada's desire to preserve a maximum degree of independence". Can the Minister explain why Mitchell Sharp's arguments have been rejected by the Cabinet, and why they do not carry weight with the Cabinet today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO EXPAND SECTORAL FREE TRADE WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is comparing apples and oranges, but I am delighted to see him interested in the vital field of expanding our trade opportunities. What Mitchell Sharp rejected and what the Government rejected was the question of total free trade with the United States or, if you like, a customs union. What I am talking about at the
present time is an examination of sectors where a free trade arrangement might be mutually beneficial to Canada and the United States, as has proved to be the case in the automotive business over the course of the past 20 years.
Right now we are looking at the question of whether it would be of advantage in relation to jobs in Canada for us to have a free trade arrangement with the United States in specialty steel, or in textiles and garments. We are also looking at the question of mass communications equipment in cities. Another possible area of examination is the petrochemical industry. The people who are in those industries and who create the jobs believe that there might be some advantages in both of those fields. It may be that our American friends will have others to suggest, but what is at stake is the free access of particular products to the vast American market which overcomes the disadvantage that Canadian manufacturers have of a very limited domestic market.

Madam Speaker, despite the wind, the Minister has not answered the question. I want to know why the federal Government is leaning away from the third option, the option to diversify our trade, which was advocated by the federal Government years ago, as well as by the Diefenbaker Government before that, in favour of a more narrow sector by sector approach with the United States at a time when, ironically, America's share of world trade and output is declining and the share of trade and output of other countries is on the way up. Why this shift at this particular time?
Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister of State (International
Trade)): Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member should realize that there is no shift. If you are running a store, you want to sell to every possible customer, particularly to customers who have the money to buy the goods. We are seeking an expansion of our trade with the United States, trying to overcome any trade barriers by the lowering of tariffs so that we can get them in there better. That does not mean that we are in any way decreasing our pursuit of Pacific Rim opportunities where the ASEAN countries and other countries have very rapid rates of growth and, therefore, are becoming better and better markets. My attitude is, let us sell Canadian goods and services to the world wherever we can, keeping in mind that export markets are shifting targets. Therefore we must shift our efforts as the opportunities occur. That is why Canadian trade has grown from $17 billion in 1970 to $85 billion last year.

subsubtopic: DISPOSITION OF BILL C-155 AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it seems that the Soviet Embassy is treating the Parliament with the same degree of contempt that has been accepted by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). However, that is not my point of order.
My point of order deals with items now standing on today's Order Paper, and it will be brief. I am raising it at this time in order to facilitate the orderly conduct of the business of the House which will arise tomorrow.
It is a well established practice of the House and one that is set out in Standing Order 79(10) that when a Bill first comes up for debate at the report stage, the Speaker has the authority to select and combine amendments for debate and often has cause to rule on the procedural acceptability or unacceptability of any or all of the amendments.
There are currently, Madam Speaker, as of today's Order Paper, some 145 notices of amendments to Bill C-155 standing on the Order Paper and, of course, there is the potential for still more amendments to be added prior to the consideration of the Bill tomorrow. I am concerned, as I am sure are the Chair and the officers of the Table, that the sheer volume of amendments for which notice has been given and the lack of notice that Members are given prior to the Chair's observations concerning the procedural acceptability of report stage amendments will combine to slow progress of debate on Bill C-155.
If I may, Madam Speaker, direct your attention to a ruling made at page 2651 of Hansard for March 27, 1973, by the then Acting Speaker, Mr. Laniel, I think that it will help to clarify the point that I am making concerning the consideration of Bill C-155 tomorrow. At that time, the Acting Speaker was ruling on the acceptability of five amendments that were put forward by Members of the Social Credit Party. He noted that Members had the undoubted right to comment on the procedural acceptability of their amendments but they should direct their observations on any given procedural point to all motions affected by a procedure, practice or rule at once rather than dealing with the amendments one by one. The Acting Speaker said, as reported at page 2651 of Hansard:
The Hon. Member naturally has a right to comment on each of these motions. The Chair considers that the notices of motions are definitely interrelated, and I think therefore that I can say straight away, on my own initiative, that the reasons behind the ruling that I propose to make concerning the five motions are based on Standing orders, and have precedents in previous rulings and opinions, or in interpretations of Standing orders in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. I do not see why the Chair should have to make a ruling on any one motion in isolation.
Considering the number of amendments that may be on the Order Paper by tomorrow and recognizing that some of those amendments will most lfkely be questionable, I suspect that both the Chair and Members will face a considerable task when attempting to straighten out the arguments being made, if in fact motions are grouped for consideration prior to
September 28, 1983

inviting the input of Hon. Members with respect to the acceptability or unacceptability of each of the amendments.
Moreover, until such time as Hon. Members have had the opportunity to study the Chair's comments with respect to the proposed amendments, it will be difficult to respond to the Chair's concerns, which undoubtedly will be raised with respect to their acceptance or non-acceptance. I would therefore put forward the suggestion, Madam Speaker, that members be given the opportunity to defend the procedural acceptability of the notices of amendments that are on the Order Paper in their name at the time those amendments would ordinarily come up for debate. This would serve to deal with procedural arguments in a more orderly manner than if all arguments were to be heard at the beginning of the debate, and indeed it might assist the Chair by focusing the arguments being made by Members to a particular procedural point.
As well, my suggestion should give Hon. Members the opportunity to study your remarks on the proposed amendments before making their submissions to the Chair, and it would alleviate the kind of uncertainty that occurred at the time when Bill C-124 came before the House and when you, Madam Speaker, were in the Chair. I am sure you will recall that that legislation had to do with the capping of civil service pensions. At that time, the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) was, through your generosity and that of the House and indeed with the consent of the House, allowed to turn back the clock and make an intervention with respect to Motion No.
1 then standing in his name at a point when debate had already progressed to the consideration of Motion No. 4.
I will not develop that point in any further detail other than to refer the Chair to Hansard of July 30, 1982, at page 19866 and subsequent pages. I will perhaps read one brief quote from Hansard because the language used was so delightful, Madam Speaker. I am quoting you, Madam Speaker, from page 19959:
It is quite a dilemma because I have just given an interpretation of what my ruling said, and in my view it meant that I had ruled. If the House did not understand what I meant, I suppose there is nothing wrong with being generous.
You then asked for the consent of the House, and the Hon. Member for Churchill was allowed to develop his argument, which you then took under consideration, Madam Speaker, and subsequently ruled upon.
1 would suggest, Madam Speaker, that before the announcement is made by the Chair, as such announcement inevitably will be made with respect to the grouping of the amendments, Members be allowed to present their submissions with respect to the acceptability or unacceptability of any of those motions within an intended grouping that may be of questionable procedural acceptability. In that way I think the procedural discussion, at least, would go ahead in a more orderly fashion. If that alternative is not accepted, then we agree that, even if the grouping occurs before the calling for submissions on the procedural acceptability or non-acceptability, it be clearly understood that Members could make submissions on each of the amendments the Chair intends to question procedurally.
Business of the House
I know that my next suggestion would place quite a burden on the Chair and the Table officers, having to deal overnight with 145, and possibly more, notices of motions bringing amendments to this measure but 1 wonder if, before the grouping tomorrow, the Chair might point out, as far as is possible, those amendments which might cause the Chair some concern with respect to their acceptability or non-acceptability. That could be taken as a signal to Members that they could work up their submissions in that regard.
1 have other concerns with respect to the interpretation of Standing Order 79(6) and the form of the notices of motions that have been filed under that Standing Order, but I can deal with those seriatim as they arise, as I expect they will, in the order in which they appear on today's Order Paper.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: DISPOSITION OF BILL C-155 AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to speak to this point of order. I feel that the interpretation of the Standing Order given by the Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is exaggerated, and I can not subscribe at all to his suggestion on how to interpret the Standing Order, which in my view is quite clear and gives the Chair full discretionary powers. The fact, however, that Standing Order 79(10) gives the Chair this power and discretion does not alter the fact that according to parliamentary practice and other Standing Orders, Hon. Members are not allowed to discuss, comment on, or appeal, the rulings of the Chair. Perhaps I may remind the Chair, since I know, Madam Speaker, that you will read over the comments made by the Member for Yukon and will also take the time to read this particular Standing Order, which is quite clear, perhaps I may draw your attention to the paragraph in question which, basically, says two things: first, it gives the Speaker the power to select or combine amendments and clauses to be proposed at the report stage.
The Standing Order also gives the Speaker, and this is where the interpretation given by the Member for Yukon runs counter to the Standing Order of the House, to what this Standing Order empowers the Speaker to do, it is the power, freedom and discretion, in case of doubt, to call upon any Member who has given the Chair notice of an amendment to give such explanation of the subject of the amendment as may enable the Speaker to form a judgment upon it. There are two aspects here: the Speaker may combine or select the amendments, and once the Chair's decision is made, it cannot be discussed or appealed in the House; the second power conferred on the Speaker by Standing Order 79(10) is probably based on concern for full consideration of the matter and for ensuring that members proposing the amendments are treated in a just and equitable manner-that the Speaker is free to consult Hon. Members until the debate begins, within the period prescribed by the Standing Orders, that is, the Speaker may call upon Members and ask them for explanations, and that should be sufficient for the Chair to draw its conclusions and make a ruling, and decide whether an amendment is acceptable or not.

September 28, 1983

As for suggesting that the Chair reverse its ruling because, with or without consultation, it had decided that an amendment was unacceptable, as for raising a point of order and having a debate on each amendment or several or a few or only one, I submit this goes against parliamentary practice, because Hon. Members may not appeal a ruling by the Chair, and the Standing Order is quite clear, and empowers the Speaker, and I quote:
-to form a judgment upon the subject of the amendment.
Once the Chair has formed a judgment, it can no longer be discussed, and we intend to respect the Standing Order. I do not agree at all with the interpretation given by my learned colleague from Yukon. In fact, I think he is giving us notice of a procedural debate that could take weeks and months-it is very easy to paralyze Parliament. The equity he is seeking, and the concern-if he is sincere, and 1 do not doubt that he is-he seems to have that each amendment, even if there are a great many, be given serious consideration, all that is covered by the Standing Order. With due respect, I submit that the Chair must consider the amendments within the limits prescribed by the Standing Order and not according to the interpretation preferred by a Member of the Opposition. In other words, if the Chair has any doubts, it can consult with any Member of this House, but once the Chair has formed a judgment, I submit that we should not waste any more of the time of the House on discussing that judgment. We have no right to discuss it. In the circumstances, I submit that we should apply Standing Order 79(10) very strictly. That is the appropriate procedure, contained in the Standing Orders of the House of Commons of Canada.

subsubtopic: DISPOSITION OF BILL C-155 AMENDMENTS

Madam Speaker, I am sure the Government House Leader did not intentionally distort what 1 said. I agree with everything he has said with respect to the interpretation of the rules-everything. I am not suggesting that the Chair should not have the discretion to group; of course the Chair has that discretion. What I am suggesting is that if the Chair has a concern about any particular amendment, then the Member in whose name that amendment stands should be given the opportunity to make submissions with respect to its procedural acceptability. We have already established precedents, and I read from them, to the effect that once amendments have been grouped, that procedure is not available to Members. It is on that fine point that I raise this problem.
In justice and fairness, Members of the House should have the right to make submissions with respect to amendments with which the Chair has concern before they are grouped, or there should be a clear understanding that it can be done after they are grouped. No one questions the discretion of the Chair to direct the grouping.

subsubtopic: DISPOSITION OF BILL C-155 AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I am not going to repeat what I said before, but I was in fact talking about this particular point. The powers the Chair has are conferred upon it by the Standing Orders. Of course, Hon. Members proposing the amendments may be consulted if the Chair so decides, but it is not up to them to decide. The consultations provided under Standing Order 79(10) cannot be imposed on the Chair by Hon. Members. If, after consultations or on its own initiative, the Chair decides that it requires explanations before making a decision, it is free to call upon Hon. Members before eleven o'clock tomorrow morning. That is what the Standing Order says. The consultation process is limited by the Standing Order, and I submit that we should follow this very clear interpretation of Standing Order 79(10). I submit that this would be a tremendous waste of Parliament's time, because it would be, and it is, against the letter and the intent of the Standing Order. The Hon. Member may be consulted, if the Chair so decides, before 11 o'clock tomorrow morning, as provided in paragraph (10) of the Standing Order.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, that is not what I have been saying at all. I guess the trouble must be the difference between my anglo thinking and the Hon. Member's franco thinking. It is only those amendments which raise questions in the mind of the Chair that will become the subject of discussion. I am suggesting to you, however, that certainly the traditions and practices of this place would seem to indicate that the Chair would want to be assisted and that the Chair would want to hear some degree of submissions with respect to the procedural non-acceptability of an amendment, if for no other reason than either fortify, or otherwise, the conclusions which she has reached on the advice of her Table officers. That is all that I am suggesting.

subsubtopic: CONVEYANCE OF HOUSE RESOLUTION TO U.S.S.R. SUPREME SOVIET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order with respect to your earlier announcement in connection with your inability to comply, as you indicated, with the resolution passed by this House on September 12. This House showed its concern by adopting a unanimous resolution to convey to the Chairman of the Presidium of the U.S.S.R. Supreme Soviet our condemnation of the act of the Government of the Supreme Soviet, and demanding, among other things, compensation to the families of those persons who lost their lives in that action.
With all respect to the Chair, may I suggest that the mere affront to this House which was committed by the Charge d'Affaires of the Soviet embassy in Canada ought not to end the matter. The final paragraph of that unanimous resolution specifically provides as follows:
Directs the Speaker to convey the text of this motion to the Chairman of the Presidium of the U.S.S.R. Supreme Soviet.
That specific direction did not require the Chair to deliver the text of the motion to the Embassy of the Soviet Union for transmittal to the Chairman of the Supreme Soviet, but rather simply to convey the text of the motion, leaving it up to the Chair to determine the mode of conveyance.
May I be permitted to submit to the Chair that there are a number of ways in which this conveyance might be undertaken? 1 am thinking specifically of a delivery of same through diplomatic pouch to the Canadian Ambassador in Moscow for delivery by hand, if necessary, coupled with a copy of that same motion to be mailed in the Soviet Union to the Chairman of the Supreme Soviet, coupled with an action by the Chair to use the Canadian mails for the purpose of mailing same to the Supreme Soviet.
1 submit to the Chair that the efforts of this House in a matter of this nature ought not to be frustrated by the actions of some underling diplomat of a foreign government who is

House Resolution
about to be reprimanded by this House of Commons. Accordingly, 1 urge upon the Chair an undertaking of the specific directions given by this House to the Chair. Some of the methods of conveyance to which I made reference certainly do not exhaust all of the methods which might be employed. I am convinced that if Madam Speaker puts her mind to it, others can be devised. My urging upon Madam Speaker is that we do not let this matter lie dormant, having regard to the concerns of all Hon. Members of the House who were involved in the passage of that unanimous resolution.

subsubtopic: CONVEYANCE OF HOUSE RESOLUTION TO U.S.S.R. SUPREME SOVIET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on the same point of order as the mover of the motion. 1 would like to say, as one Hon. Member of Parliament, that 1 am deeply disturbed by what can only be described as a contemptuous action by the Soviet Union with regard to this motion. If I heard your honour correctly, and I think 1 did, in reporting back to the House, the Charge d'Affaires of the Soviet Union had been instructed, presumably by his superiors in the Soviet Union, not to accept this message which was passed by the Parliament of Canada.
I repeat, Madam Speaker, in my view that amounts to a contempt of Parliament. It is to compound the mistaken, villainous or cruel act, however one wants to describe it-and I believe all of those adjectives are appropriate to describe the original action of the shooting down of a civilian aircraft by the Soviet Union-for the Soviet Union to respond in this way.
I also feel very seriously, Madam Speaker, that the Parliament of Canada cannot let the matter stand with our having received from the Chair a message from the Charge d'Affaires. I would like to say that I, for one, feel the course of action that Your Honour has taken was the appropriate one, the initial step, and I am, frankly, astounded and surprised that no matter what it thought of the content of the message, the Soviet Union has seen fit simply not to receive it.
1 feel, Madam Speaker, in addition to some suggestions which have been made now about subsequent action, that it would probably be appropriate for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) on behalf of the Government of Canada to request now that the Charge d'Affaires come to him, as the appropriate Minister in the Government of Canada, to explain why such contemptuous behaviour should be taken by the Soviet Union, which, I repeat, amounts to a contempt of this Parliament. That resolution was unanimously passed. It reflected the very serious, deeply felt feelings of the people of Canada. The very least the Soviet Union ought to do is to receive the message before it responds to it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CONVEYANCE OF HOUSE RESOLUTION TO U.S.S.R. SUPREME SOVIET
speechtext:
I am quite grateful for these suggestions which have been made by the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Gamble). However, I will address myself to the last suggestion made by the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). I do not feel that I can delegate this responsibility to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), who would be speaking in the name of the Government about a resolution which the Parliament of Canada has asked the Speaker to transmit to the Soviet authorities.

September 28, 1983
House Resolution
The effect of the order given to the Chair by the House is that the Charge d'Affaires did not accept it. We know the answer. I do not believe it would be useful for me to ask, and I would not delegate that responsibility to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. If the Minister wants to pick that up on his own and initiate some kind of action, of course, he is free to do so. However, 1 will look into the other suggestions to see how this message can be transmitted. We already know that a message which was transmitted by the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not been received, has been refused, here in Ottawa. Also a message which was conveyed by our Embassy in Moscow was refused.
1 can go that route myself, following the suggestions of the Hon. Members. However, I repeat, I would not delegate that responsibility to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I do not feel it would be proper for Parliament to delegate that responsibility, unless the House decides unanimously otherwise. I do not see that it is implicit in the order which this Parliament has given me that 1 now go to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and ask him to perform that duty for me.

subsubtopic: CONVEYANCE OF HOUSE RESOLUTION TO U.S.S.R. SUPREME SOVIET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not think I said that you, yourself, should request the Secretary of State for External Affairs to take that step. If I did say that, I did not mean to. But I do believe he should do it, and that, quite correctly, should come as a request from some of us on this side of the House. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) is here; he might indicate he is in agreement with the suggestion and take it to the Minister.
The reason 1 think it should now be raised with the Minister is that I regard the initial response of the Soviet Union as a contempt of Parliament. We have already seen that it does not intend to respond to the highest officer of this Parliament and therefore is not likely to take any other appropriate action. As a result of that, my view is that we now have to shift the focus. The Soviet Union has taken an additional step to the original one in indicating it is not even prepared to listen to the Parliament of Canada. I think that is a very serious mistake. It is a contempt for any Government which has representatives in this country of ours to so treat Parliament. It is very serious indeed.
Some Hon. Members; Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONVEYANCE OF HOUSE RESOLUTION TO U.S.S.R. SUPREME SOVIET
speechtext: It is my view that the Secretary of State for External Affairs ought to be calling in the Charge d'Affaires to pass on this message that we view with contempt, if you like, their contemptuous behaviour.

1 would have another suggestion to offer to you, Madam Speaker. Since the Soviet diplomats are in contempt of this House, 1 suggest that you inform each one of them that he or she is persona non grata in the galleries of this House until the message from this House has been accepted by them.

subsubtopic: AM STEREO IN CANADA
speechtext:
1.	Is the Government prepared to allow the speedy introduction of AM stereo in Canada and, if so, on what date?

subsubtopic: AM STEREO IN CANADA
speechtext:
In so far
as the Department of Communications is concerned, the reply to the above question is as follows:
1.	The Government has issued experimental authorizations to broadcasters in various parts of the country to test a number of different AM stereophonic systems. The results of these experiments are being reviewed by three different consultative groups including a specialized committee of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, the Technical Advisory Committee of the Department of Communications, and the Canadian Radio Technical Planning Board. Upon an analysis of these experimental results and based on the recommendations of these consultative groups, it is expected that AM stereo will be introduced in Canada in a timely manner.
2.	One of the most recent technological breakthroughs in the field of AM stereophonic broadcasting has been in the development of multisystem receivers capable of decoding any of the systems which are currently available. The technical committees are reviewing this new development and will make recommendations concerning the cost effectiveness and technical acceptability of these receivers for the Canadian market. Should these recommendations be favourable and in the public interest, the Department will consider the development of regulations whereby only "universal" type AM stereo receivers would be allowed to be sold in Canada.

That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act in order that, a once-in-a-lifctime exemption from capital gains taxation be provided for the main business property of non-incorporated or incorporated farmers and businesses employing less than 30 persons, and with gross sales less than $1 million annually, and with fewer than three places of business, excluding foreign-owned farms or businesses, franchise operations and quota values of any kind, and this exemption from capital gains be made conditional upon those involved investing at least 50 per cent of the taxable amount in the Farm Credit Corporation or in Small Business Development Bonds, at a rate of interest to be more than 50 per cent of the Canadian prime interest rate.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with substantial pleasure that I rise to speak briefly on the motion today, because 1 believe the fact that 1 am able to raise this issue and to cause some deliberation of this proposal by Hon. Members on all sides of the House is a reflection that the process in Canada continues to work and that individuals at the grass roots level can have the opportunity to have their ideas contemplated and promoted by themselves, and then deliberated by the House.
1 want to pay particular tribute to a farmer in my constituency, an immigrant to Canada from Belgium some many years ago by the name of Leon Meersseman who, while growing tobacco on his property, cultivating his fields, expresses his concern with respect to the quality of life in Canada and how it may somehow be improved for other Canadians by giving thought to the tax system, among other things, as reflected in this particular motion. I wish I could claim its complete authorship. 1 wish, that I could stand before Hon. Members today and suggest that this idea had its genesis in my own conciousness, but it was in fact this farmer who initially came to me with the idea. It was probably generated from thoughts being put forth by Members of this House and by the Government when we were debating alternative sources of funding for the Farm Credit Corporation and the concept of Small Business Bonds to assist not only small businessmen but also the farming operations in Canada.
I think it is a fact accepted by Hon. Members on all sides of the House that we are currently in a time in our society when there is a tremendous impact upon farmers and small businessmen of high interest rates and of the effect of an ever-restric-tive credit market to which they can go not only for their ongoing daily operations but for their long-term credit as well. Indeed, this House has expressed itself on a number of occasions in supporting the Small Business Bond concept.
In supporting the extension of sources from which farm credit could be seeking its funds, allowing it to go to the private market, and in coming forward with this particular Bill, the idea in mind, in simple form, was to permit Canadians to invest in themselves, in particular, to allow small businessmen and farmers to invest in their own operations and to come to the assistance of others who find themselves in the same employ. In effect, through this motion we are asking the Government to contemplate permitting farmers to fund the FCC themselves, at least in part. In order to effect that, we are

Agreed.

September 28, 1983
Capital Gains Tax attempting to alleviate what, at the very least, is an irritant in my view and in the minds of most of those in the farming community of Canada, namely the capital gains tax.
While making this proposal to the House, it is not without recognition of the fact that this country had provisions for inheritance taxes and state taxes. One can place it in this context, that the society that we represent bought the removal of those inheritance and succession duty taxes by the acceptance of the concept of the capital gains tax. However, there are certain problems with that kind of taxation. Farmers, in particular, and certainly in the same sort of way the small businessman, are the engines of this nation who create employment and provide the food which would otherwise not be placed on our tables. They are in a different position from that of the labourer or the salaried employees who have the opportunity, through other tax provisions such as RRSPs, RHOSPs and the other mechanisms the House has put into our tax system, to set aside money for their retirement. I believe Members from all sides of the House accept the principle that farmers and small businessmen find their retirement programs in their farms and businesses since they do not have the disposable income from their business operations to permit them to purchase RRSPs or other retirement plans for their advanced years. They are unable to take advantage of tax incentives to save money in that manner.
With respect to farmers, they use their money for the improvement of their land or buildings in an attempt to enhance their operations and make them more viable, or to become more efficient producers. Therefore, at the end of their working lives they find that what others would have put away for retirement they have used on their farming operations. When that operation is sold they are exposed to the capital gains tax.
1 think it is probably charitable to express that as an irritant. In many instances it is far beyond an irritation. While exemptions have been provided to permit tranferral to members of the family, there are still farmers in our society with no sons or daughters to whom those transfers can be made. Not only do those individuals lose the ability to make that rollover, they are subjected to a tax which they view as a robbery of their ability to look after themselves in their old age.
Therefore, this motion attempts to achieve two goals. It attempts to provide funding for the FCC and small business development from the private sector while providing an exemption or relief from the total effect of the capital gains tax at the same time. The motion suggests that there be a minimum investment and that only a portion of the investment be subjected to a preferred tax. The return from that investment should be lower than the standard rate of interest so that it is not viewed as a windfall but rather a conscious decision on the part of the investors not only to protect themselves for the future in some small way but to help those who may want to continue the occupation they loved throughout their working life.
1 recognize that 1 do not have the benefit of the Finance Department to analyze all the financial implications of this proposal. However, 1 put it to the House that my idea has sufficient merit at least to bear discussion and examination by the Finance Department as well as a response in the House, in the event it is found unacceptable, to explain why it is so. It should not simply be said to be unacceptable without its conceptual problems being disclosed.
I believe this concept will work. It is not so novel as to be completely unheard of. It probably bears some similarity to the agri-bond proposals of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, which are not without some merit. That concept certainly bears some consideration, and I am not married to this proposal in the sense that I would be opposed to an alternative such as an agri-bond issue or other proposal which would achieve the same end.
I am attempting to sensitize Members of the House, and hopefully the bureaucracy, to the idea that there is a need in the country and that the public would like to see us working on this or similar ideas that would achieve the same end.
At the end of the day, if I could have achieved that, I believe I will have achieved the end to which I alluded at the beginning, that is, that our system permits the upward movement of an idea from the fields in Essex County to the point where the House could express its views upon it, then into the bowels of the bureaucracy, hopefully to be generated back to the House in this or some other form so that we could see legislation implemented.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent (Mr. Daudlin) for doing some thinking. While I would not suggest naturally that all of his thoughts were the same as those of others, he has touched the central theme that small business persons and farmers across the country have been expressing to their Members of Parliament at least since prior to 1971. The theme is that capital gains taxation affects them negatively. Furthermore, they perceive it as being unfair, as do most representatives.
I submit that we do not have the concept called capital gains tax today. That is, we do not have a tax on gains. Instead, it is a tax on gain plus inflation.
Let us use the farming business as an example. Since valuation day is 1971, a tractor purchased in 1971 may sell today for more than its purchase price. But surely there is not a Member sitting in the House today who believes that that tractor is in fact worth more today than it was more than a decade ago after it may have had as many as a thousand hours of use. That tractor, which has less new technology, less comfort and more wear, is not worth more. The fact is the inflation has added phoney, or funny, money. Therefore, the sale price simply indicates a number that looks larger but does not, in reality, represent a greater value. Therefore, that is not a capital gains tax but a capital gain plus inflation tax.
What other segment of our society is paying tax on inflation? More important, farmers are among the only group of
September 28, 1983

business persons in the entire country who can not protect themselves against inflation. For example, if that tax were applied to a clothing store operator, and his cost to purchase clothing for the store increased, he would simply sell the clothing for more. Whoever heard of a farmer saying that his gasoline costs him 30 per cent more this year so his wheat will be sold for 30 per cent more? Whoever heard of a farmer, after hearing feedgrain costs had risen, selling his meat for a certain amount more? Farmers must pay the price on the products they buy and they receive the price that is offered to them when they sell. Therefore, there is a double jeopardy where farmers are not only the only group in society which is taxed on inflation, but are one of the groups in society that cannot protect themselves against inflation.
The Government needs to listen to the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent who sits on its side of the House. I am pleased that this piece of legislation is in his name. According to the rules for Private Members' Motions, if we speak beyond an hour this piece of legislation will have been spoken out. I am pleased to follow the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent because I do not want to speak out this motion. 1 think it deserves the consideration which he requests. I have some trouble with the last part of it because I do not believe we have the right to tell farmers to invest in the Farm Credit Corporation. 1 think they are subjected to a phoney taxation now, but at least the motion of the Hon. Member is better than the present case.
Canadians listening to the debate today on television or those who will read it in Hansard in the future should know that whatever Member talks out this motion will have to bear the burden. It is upon his or her shoulders if this good piece of legislation does not go forward.
As the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent indicated, farmers are faced with a tax on inflation. Also it should be pointed out that of all the tax systems in Canada today, the capital gains tax is the most expensive to collect. In the case of income tax, people sit in their homes, fill out their forms, mail them in, and once they are audited and checked by the Department of National Revenue, that is the amount they receive from or owe the Government. In the case of the capital gains tax, the Government is dealing with acquired properties and assessed values. It requires a bank and battery of assessors and inspectors, and an entire new process of collecting the tax dollar is created. The fundamental question is not whether it is more expensive to farmers, but whether it is justified in the first place. To be truthful, if a farmer did not pay his capital gains tax, that money would be recorded as income and would be subject to income tax. Surely one should not have to pay income tax and be exposed to the capital gains tax at the same time.
What a whipping of our farmers who are the most efficient producers in Canada! Anyone who doubts that should read the speeches of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in which he praised the efficiency of farmers compared with other Canadian producers. In his great rhetoric of "irregard-less" and "et cetera", he talked about how efficient farmers
Capital Gains Tax
were. The Government of Canada does not believe that because it treats them in a totally unfair manner in terms of taxation and capital gains.
With the capital gains tax on farmland, I believe we have a double jeopardy in taxation. For example, if a farmer purchased a new parcel of land in 1975 at a fixed value of $1,000 per acre, and if he sold it in 1983 at $1,500 per acre, the $500 difference would be called profit and subjected to taxation. But in 1975 he used money on which he had already paid income tax to purchase the land. If he is taxed when he sells the land, then he has actually been taxed twice. If we look at the question of gains, we must analyse whether or not it was a gain or whether the gain was inflation. If the gain was simply inflation, then he is certainly being taxed twice.
There are many examples in the agricultural and small business sectors of something being called gain which is not gain but in fact is double taxation or prejudice against a sector of society which the Minister of Agriculture frequently claims is the most efficient in the country today.
Those of us who have the privilege of serving rural communities-and the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent serves a rural community-occasionally hear our city cousins in coffee shops talk about, "the rich farmer".
Oh!
I hear an Hon. Member of the NDP making noises. It is amazing how 11 per cent of the membership of the House of Commons makes more than 50 per cent of the noise.
Especially with 20 per cent of the vote.
There he goes again. He referred to 11 per cent of the vote in the next election.
1 said, "20 per cent".

In any event, when we hear our city cousins talking about "rich farmers", they fail to realize that farmers do not only work eight hours per day, five days per week. Also our urban cousins fail to remember that there are more than one or two breadwinners in farming families. Their hours per day and their days per week are longer. Many family members are involved in the task of producing goods, yet farms are taxed as if they were some other business, all within a year's calendar and as if all the money were one earning. This productive sector of our society is being taxed in an unusually harsh manner.
Before taking my seat, I want to indicate that 1 am deeply annoyed with the way in which we have developed, both federally and provincially, discrimination against rural people. I am not only referring to the example of capital gains which affects mostly farmers. 1 am also referring to the rates of telephone companies. Our urban cousins, depending upon the Province, receive this service for $6 or $8 per private telephone per month, whereas farmers are forced to make deals on $100,000 combines while four of his neighbours listen in. In my constituency, which is mainly involved in ranching, there is

September 28, 1983
Capital Gains Tax
a move to take away rural mail service. Some ranches are 60 miles apart in the southern part of my riding. Yet our urban cousins receive door-to-door delivery from Canada Post. They can simply get out of bed, go to the door and reach around the corner to grab their mail. This is somehow deemed to be fair by Canada Post, by Mr. Warren. I submit that it is not. Turning to telecommunications or television service, in east central Alberta and west central Saskatchewan, this service is absolutely atrocious. There are communities which do not receive adequate television, despite the fact that the residents of Frobisher Bay receive six television channels. I believe there is discrimination against the rural sector of Canada.
Very few groups in society, except farmers and some small business persons, pay tax on inflation, pay double jeopardy tax, and have their retirement funds stolen. The Hon. Member for Essex-Kent mentioned the point as well that when a farmer acquires his property, in effect he is hoping that someday, when he receives his capital, it will be his nestegg for his retirement years. In comes the Government, big fisted, grabbing half of what the farmer has brought in, claiming that the farmer's retirement fund belongs to it.
All Members should accept the motion put forward. It merely states that "the Government should consider the advisability". Whether it is right or not in all of the specifics, the Government should consider the advisability of taking a new look at the capital gains question. 1 remind all Hon. Members that the last person to speak, if he speaks for the full hour, has upon his shoulders the burden of upsetting this initiative of questioning its acceptability. That should not occur. This Bill should be allowed to pass so that we can give due consideration to an injustice which has existed for more than a decade. That has been far too long a period, and should not continue to exist.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Essex Kent (Mr. Daudlin) to study the whole question of the capital gains tax as it affects farmers and small businessmen. This has been of concern to those in rural communities in particular ever since it began to develop as an uneven or unequal form of taxation, starting in about the mid-seventies.
Members of the House do not easily forget the promise made by the governing Party in the last election to attempt to ameliorate the situation. I remind the House that the promise was to change the evaluation day from December 31, 1971 to an evaluation day in 1974. Some of their literature indicated that an indexing provision would be applied as well.
Since coming here, prior to every budget I have written a letter to the Minister of Finance. This is one of three or four items included in my letter. So far it has been ignored by Ministers of Finance. Because the item has again come up for debate today, 1 hope that in a subsequent budget the Minister will recall one of the few campaign promises affecting small business and agriculture which his Party made at the time of
the last election. It was part of the mandate. It is time that that small amelioration of excess taxation in this regard be looked at.
We got into this position on what seemed to be fairly rational grounds. The Carter Commission investigated the whole taxation system. It was to come up with a system that would tax everyone equitably. Carter made the very succinct statement that a buck is a buck and it should be taxed. Unfortunately, 10 or 12 years later we do not have a much better situation than at the time of the Carter investigation. We have wobbled away from any attempt to have equitable taxation and have gone back to ad hockery at its finest in every budget since then. It is very timely that the House consider this motion, which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act in order that a once-in-a-lifetime exemption from capital gains taxation be provided for the main business property of non-incorporated or incorporated farmers and businesses employing less than 30 persons, and with growth sales less than $1 million annually, and with fewer than three places of business, excluding foreign-owned farms or business, franchise operations and quota values of any kind, and this exemption from capital gains be made conditional upon those involved investing at least 50 per cent of the taxable amount in the Farm Credit Corporation or in Small Business Development Bonds, at a rate of interest to be more than 50 per cent of the Canadian prime interest rate.
That is a very good area of study, something that should be a primary objective of the House in the next few months. Many questions are raised in this motion which require further study and investigation. Included in the items for study is the whole question of the ownership of farmland and the relationship between professional and business investment in farmland as a hedge against inflation.
The taxation system will have to address the question of whether the investment is simply a hedge against inflation. In recent years, up until last year, the value of farmland has increased faster than the average rate of inflation. This has been the case for the past six or eight years. It has been a good investment for a professional or someone operating another business to provide himself with a hedge against inflation. The problem is the effect that this has on rural communities and farmers attempting to use their investment in farmland as a means of making a living. Sometimes the requirements or expectations of the two groups are quite different.
The farmer buys the land in order to generate income and provide himself and his family with a living. The investors invest because recent experience has proven that the investment will not deteriorate very quickly. The question is whether they should be treated equally when it comes to taxation.
Another question is whether we should continue with some of the ad hoc solutions thrown into the capital gains aspect as it affects farmers and small businesses. For example, will the in-family rollover continue, or should that be studied as well? When we look at capital gains, we should also look at how Revenue Canada treats farmers. That should be put under intense scrutiny as well. The definitions that Revenue Canada is using for those attempting to become farmers and the distinctions they are making between those who are genuinely attempting to begin farming by having an off-farm job and
September 28, 1983

those people they consider to be using a farm as a means of avoiding taxation are questionable, to say the least. 1 have had cases in my riding where a farmer has been farming for 45 or 46 years. That farmer is now in his middle sixties. He has turned over by sale some of his property to his sons and daughters. He still farms 700 acres or 800 acres but, for some reason, Revenue Canada has decided that he is no longer a farmer. The reasons for this are not too clear. He is, however, being taxed as a non-farmer and he is not being allowed to deduct some of the farm expenses that he has had in the profession that he has carried out for all of his life. Those are the kinds of things that must be clarified and made consistent if equity is to be introduced into the taxation system as it affects small business people and farmers.
Are the limits that are proposed here indeed the best limits that could be proposed? Are they workable right across the country? Are they workable in the farm community as well as in the small business community? The limit of $1 million for total actual turnover of gross sales means different things for different businesses. For instance, even within the farming sector, there is a wide variation between gross sales and the actual amount of investment that the farmer will have.
If a farmer engages in an intensive livestock feeding operation, his gross sales could meet or even occasionally exceed the amount of money that he has invested. However, for prairie grain farms at the present time, and 1 think the same would hold true for cropping operations in central Canada and maritime Canada, gross sales under current market conditions are equivalent to about 10 per cent of the investment. In other words, if a grain farm in western Canada, under average conditions in western Canada today, were to generate gross sales of $1 million, we would probably be looking at an operation that would have an investment of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $10 million. With the mechanization that is often present in that particular branch of farming, the operation would not employ anything approaching 30 people but would perhaps employ more like eight or ten people.
The question of what limits to impose and what criteria to use should, I think, be studied and not accepted as given, as may be the interpretation of this particular motion. I would hope, if it does get to a committee of some sort of special consideration, that all of these proposed limitations be treated simply as proposals and that such a committee would work diligently to come up with a more equitable kind of taxing system, not only in the area of capital gains but also investigate the taxing system as it affects small businessmen and farmers in general.
The proposal to provide some sort of reinvestment funding through the purchase of a form of agri-bond that seems to be present in this motion is something that is definitely worth further study. It is something that has been called for by many farm organizations and some of the business communities. This proposal, as I read it, would give the selling farmer or small businessman the opportunity to avoid any form of capital
Capital Gains Tax
gains tax if he had apparently already made his once-in-a-lifetime sale and had some further property or business to dispose of. He would have the option of designating half of that income to an agri-bond or a special bond through the Small Business Development Bank which could be used by the next generation of small businessmen or farmers.
1 remind the House that some of the lending institutions that existed back when 1 was just beginning in my profession of farming did have a policy similar to that. At that time, Co-operative Trust in western Canada would provide loans to young farmers who had very little equity. It would provide loans to farmers with as little as 20 per cent equity, provided the seller of the farmland would invest at least half of the proceeds of the sale in Co-operative Trust investments. It was simply a requirement of the transaction that at least half of the proceeds of the sale go back into the lending institution so that it could serve an ever-increasing clientele of young beginning farmers and small businessmen.
Until such time as there is a complete review of the taxation system as it applies to small businessmen and farmers and until we have a system that would take all aspects of the taxation picture into account, as an interim measure, I would alert the House to a proposal that was made by Members from this corner of the House many times. Until such time as there is a full reassessment of the taxation policies of the country, the House would be well advised to adopt an exemption for capital gains purposes for small businessmen and farmers that would exempt the first $100,000 of the capital gain. This proposal has been implemented in at least one Province in the country. Under the previous provincial Government administration in Saskatchewan, the New Democratic Government had placed that kind of exemption on the provincial portion of capital gains tax that is levied. I think that there would be some merit to proposing a similar kind of exemption at the federal level.
As the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) mentioned, there is a measure of inequity involved in the way the taxation system affects farm people and the way it affects their urban cousins. While it appears to be equal in terms of the full exemption for the primary residence, it is a very clear economic fact that a farm house, no matter how nice it is, never achieves the same market value as does a similar home located in an urban setting. This proposed exemption on the first $100,000 of capital gain would tend to rectify the inequality that exists there.
Indexation is something that 1 think must accompany any kind of continuation of a valuation day that one must work from. While all of us in the House are, I think, in favour of indexing any valuation day that continues on in the current method of imposing tax, the problem is, which index is to be used? Is the straight cost of living index to be used or is the real valuation of the property, business or farm in that particular Province to be used?
There are wide variations from year to year between regions of the country with regard to capital gains that accrue. In the year that has just finished, many Provinces noted no captial

September 28, 1983
Capital Gains Tax
gain in the value of farmland. Many showed a negative gain with land actually dropping in value. Only one or two Provinces showed a marginal increase in the value of farmland last year. This does vary. The question of indexation, whether a property index, a business index, a combination of both or a general cost of living index, should be studied. The fact that there is no index has created a disproportionate tax load on farmers and small-businessmen who have retired under the current capital gains law, and that inequity should be corrected as soon as possible.
I recommend that a study of the whole area of taxation, particularly capital gains, should be proceeded with post haste. In the interim, there is room for patching up of the well-patched valuation day and the capital gains taxation. I think the proposals I have made today would make the law more equitable.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent (Mr. Daudlin) for bringing this motion forward today. It is a timely motion and recognizes an inequity that has been a burden on all farmers and small-businessmen across Canada. It is a tax that was imposed perhaps as a result of a series of discussions and pressures brought to bear by other sections of society that wanted the deletion of the estate tax and the implementation of a capital gains tax as an alternative. Little did the organizations that presented the proposal realize the effect the tax would have during the inflationary 1970s. As was indicated by the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), the tax could be regarded as being harsher than was intended, and in fact as being a tax on inflation. I want to commend the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent for his concern.
1 think we should look at what has happened over the years. In Alberta the total value of land and buildings increased ten times in 12 years, from 3.5 billion in 1971 to S30.2 billion in 1982; in Saskatchewan it went from $3.8 billion to $26.8 billion in the same period; in Ontario from $5.1 billion to $24.7 billion in the same period.
There is another problem, Mr. Speaker. If we are concerned about the disappearance of productive agricultural land in Canada-and obviously the Provinces, whose jurisdiction this comes under, are not doing anything about it-then we should look further than has been suggested by either Member of the Opposition who spoke. We should examine the possibility of exempting all agricultural land from capital gains tax as long as it is kept in food production. This may be the only way for the Government to prevent its disappearance if the Provinces are not going to assist in this regard. I recognize that the management of these resources comes under provincial jurisdiction.
I have to agree with the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent that over the years of their involvement, farmers and small-businessmen have reinvested in order to improve their holdings or expand their businesses and hope to use the proceeds as their retirement income. 1 believe the time has come to make some
allowance for the toll that inflation has taken of retirement savings. It is for this reason that 1 wholeheartedly endorse the motion.
I should like to suggest that perhaps it is time for the Government to look at another aspect of farm financing or of financing small businesses. We should examine the possibility of giving a guarantee to any farmer or small-businessman who would take back a mortgage on fixed capital assets, as is done with farm improvement loans or small business loans or even through Canada Mortgage and Housing. 1 wholeheartedly endorse the motion and hope it will receive speedy passage.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the motion before the House. The capital gains tax imposed on the sale of agricultural land is one of the major problems that farmers face, particularly when it comes to the continuation of the family farm. In the constituency that I represent, on valuation day in 1971 a quarter section of land sold for approximately $12,000 per quarter. Today that same property is selling for $70,000 or $80,000 per quarter. The resulting capital gains tax is a tremendous burden on the family farm and more particularly on the senior farmer who may want to retire with some dignity. If a farmer owns five or six quarter sections of land and wants to retire to settle in a small rural town in Saskatchewan, he finds that he does not have the cash available to buy a home so that he can retire with dignity. Usually he wants his son to carry on the family farm. The motion before the House would alleviate his problems to a great extent. The rollover provision in the Income Tax Act is of some help but in many cases the senior farmer just does not have the money that would allow him to retire while at the same time allowing the family farm to continue operation. The Income Tax Act has been counterproductive in many areas but if we were to single out one area where it is most counterproductive, it is in the continuation of a farm or business.
I am very pleased to support the motion and to bring to the attention of the House that for several years this Party has called for this kind of move on the part of the Government. I hope the Government will see fit to support the motion and will bring legislation to the House which will benefit the whole agricultural area, particularly the senior farmer who faces these problems.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am happy to speak to the motion although I do not agree with everything that is in it. 1 think you mentioned my name as seconder of the motion; I do not know how I got that honour. I am happy to second it but I have some reservations about portions of it.
It seems to me that we are talking about two different questions in this little motion and I think they have been mixed up and incorrectly construed in some of the speeches we have heard. We are talking, first, about capital gains tax in general. Then, more specifically, within that broad question we are talking about the indexation of the capital itself, so that the
September 28, 1983

only portion being taxed is the portion which is a real gain. If that is the principle, I certainly support it.
We have done that in other areas. We have done it with our personal income tax, which is indexed every year. We are about to introduce, on October 1, the indexed security investment plan, which will index capital gains for publicly traded shares on the stock market.
1 would like to draw to the attention of every Hon. Member a very important paper which was published in November of 1980 entitled "A Review of the Taxation of Capital Gains in Canada". On page 4 there is a very important principle stated in one brief sentence, which 1 would like to quote:
An individual who realizes a S100 gain has the same increased spending and saving alternatives as another person who receives an additional $100 in his paycheque.
That is a very important principle. There are three ways to make money in this country: first, from your pay cheque. If you are a factory worker, a school teacher, a clerk in a store, an executive or whatever, your weekly pay cheque is your first way to make money. The second way to make money is from profits from a company. The third way to make money is to invest in a capital gain and watch that gain grow.
When we heard some of the references here about capital gains tax, particularly by the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), we learned of some mistakes in the calculation of the tax liabilities on capital gains. Capital gains tax out of those three areas is the easiest tax to carry because it is a half tax. At maximum rates it is a half tax. Half the gain is brought into income and half is overlooked entirely. Then the half which is brought into income is taxed at the subsequent marginal rate. That makes the capital gain out of those three areas the easiest tax to bear because it is, first of all, only a tax on half of the profit.
Let us take the example given by the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) with respect to farmers in his area and follow it straight through, including in the example the extra provision of capital gains reserves, which makes the capital gains tax even easier to bear. Let us say that the farmer sells a quarter of his land at $80,000 profit. His total sale based on the figures which the Hon. Member gave us would be, let us say, $92,000. The farmer bought the land for $12,000 in 1971 and is selling it for $92,000 today. He has a total profit differential, inflation plus real gain, of $80,000.
